p: "וַיֵּשֶׁב יַעֲקֹב" (בְּרֵאשִׁית לז, א).
— “And Jacob dwelt” (Genesis 37:1).
בִּמְדְרַשׁ רַבָּה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פד, א) כָּתַב:
— In Midrash Rabbah (Bereishit Rabbah 84:1) it is written:
"בְּזַעֲקֵךְ יַצִּילוּךְ קִבּוּצַיִךְ" (יְשַׁעְיָה נז, יג),
— “When you cry out, let your assemblies save you” (Isaiah 57:13),
תָּנֵי: כִּינּוּסוֹ וְכִינּוּס בָּנָיו הִצִּילוּ וְכוּלֵי.
— it was taught: his gathering and the gathering of his sons saved, etc.
וְיֵשׁ לְהָבִין,
— And this needs to be understood:
בִּשְׁלָמָא כִּינּוּס בָּנָיו יִתָּכֵן,
— granted that the gathering of his sons is plausible,
אֲבָל כִּינּוּסוֹ, אֵיךְ שַׁיָּיךְ כִּינּוּס עַל נֶפֶשׁ אַחַת?
— but his own gathering, how can gathering apply to a single individual soul?
וְיוּבַן עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּמִּשְׁנָה (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כז:):
— And it can be understood based on what is written in the Mishnah (Rosh Hashanah 27b):
"זֶה כִּיוֵּון לִבּוֹ וְזֶה לֹא כִּיוֵּון לִבּוֹ",
— “This one directed his heart and that one did not direct his heart,”
וְכֵן (רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ה דִּבְרָכוֹת ל:):
— and likewise (beginning of Chapter 5 of Berakhot 30b):
"חֲסִידִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים הָיוּ שׁוֹהִין שָׁעָה אַחַת וּמִתְפַּלְּלִין
— “The early pious ones would linger for one hour and pray
כְּדֵי שֶׁיְּכַוְּונוּ אֶת לִבָּם לַאֲבִיהֶם שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם".
— so that they might direct their hearts toward their Father in Heaven.”
וּלְשׁוֹן כִּיוּוּן הוּא יַשְׁרוּת הַלֵּב,
— And the term ‘kivun’ (directed focus) denotes uprightness and alignment of the heart,
וְהוּא לְיַישֵׁר אֶת הַלֵּב שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה פָּזוּר בְּתַאֲווֹת וַחֲמָדוֹת עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
— and it means to align the heart so that it is not scattered across lusts and coveted physical desires of this world,
רַק שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מְכוּוָּן וּמְיוּשָּׁר לַאֲבִיו שֶׁבַּשָּׁמָיִם.
— but that it be focused and aligned exclusively toward its Father in Heaven.
וְאִיתָא בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (פֶּרֶק ב דִּבְרָכוֹת הֲלָכָה ד):
— And it is brought in the Yerushalmi (Berakhot 2:4):
אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא רוֹבָא:
— Rabbi Chiya the Great said:
"אֲנָא מִן יוֹמָא לָא כַּוּוֹנִית,
— “In all my days I never directed my heart,
אֶלָּא חַד זְמַן בָּעֵי מְכַוְּונָה,
— except on one occasion I wished to direct it,
וְהִרְהַרִית בְּלִבִּי וְאָמְרִי:
— and I reflected in my heart and thought:
מַאן עָלֵיל קוֹמֵי מַלְכָּא קַדְמֵי,
— who enters before the king first,
אַלְקַפְתָּא אוֹ רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא?".
— the alabarch (al-qafta) or the Exilarch (Reish Galuta)?”
שְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר:
— Shmuel said:
"אֲנָא מָנִית אַפְרוֹחַיָּא".
— “I counted fledglings.”
רַבִּי בּוּן בַּר חִיָּיא אָמַר:
— Rabbi Bun bar Chiya said:
"אֲנָא מָנִית דִּימוֹסְיָא".
— “I counted rows of building stones.”
וְהוּבָא בְּתוֹסָפוֹת (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה טז:) וּשְׁאָר רִאשׁוֹנִים.
— And this is cited in Tosafot (Rosh Hashanah 16b) and other early commentators.
וְהוּא פֶּלֶא,
— And it is an astonishing wonder
שֶׁהָאֲמוֹרָאִים לֹא יְכַוְּונוּ בִּתְפִלָּתָם,
— that the Amoraim would fail to have focused intention in their prayer,
וּבִפְרָט רַבִּי חִיָּיא רַבָּה,
— and especially Rabbi Chiya the Great,
דְּאִיתָא (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא פה:):
— concerning whom it is stated (Bava Metzia 85b):
"וְיֵשׁ דּוּגְמָתָן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה?",
— “And is there an equivalent to them in this world?”
אָמַר לוֹ: "אִיכָּא רַבִּי חִיָּיא וּבָנָיו וְכוּלֵי,
— He said to him: “There are Rabbi Chiya and his sons, etc.,
כִּי מָטֵי לְמֵימַר 'מְחַיֵּה הַמֵּתִים' רָגַשׁ עָלְמָא וְכוּלֵי", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
— when he arrived to say ‘He Who revives the dead’ the entire world shuddered, etc.”, see there.
וְהֵיאַךְ יִתָּכֵן שֶׁרַבִּי חִיָּיא יֹאמַר שֶׁלֹּא כִּיוֵּון בִּתְפִלָּה מִיָּמָיו?
— And how could it be conceivable that Rabbi Chiya would say that he never achieved focused intention in prayer in his days?
גַּם הֵיאַךְ שַׁיָּיךְ מַחֲשָׁבוֹת כָּאֵלּוּ שֶׁיְּהַרְהֵר בָּהֶן
— Furthermore, how could such thoughts enter, that he should contemplate
מַאן עָיֵיל בְּרֵישָׁא וְכוּלֵי,
— who enters first, etc.,
שֶׁיִּתָּכֵן שֶׁיִּפּוֹל בְּלֵב הַמִּתְפַּלֵּל מַחֲשָׁבוֹת מֵהִרְהוּרֵי לִבּוֹ כָּל הַיּוֹם,
— for while it is plausible that thoughts reflecting one’s daytime preoccupations might fall into a worshiper’s heart,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּ'חוֹבַת הַלְּבָבוֹת'
— as written in Chovot HaLevavot,
תַּלְמִיד חָכָם בְּעִנְיְנֵי לִימּוּדוֹ וְסוֹחֵר בְּעִנְיְנֵי עֲסָקָיו,
— a Torah scholar regarding matters of his study and a merchant regarding matters of his business,
אֲבָל עִנְיָן כָּזֶה שֶׁבֶּטַח לֹא הִרְהֵר בּוֹ, אֵיךְ נָפַל בְּלִבּוֹ בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ?
— yet such an arbitrary political matter which he certainly did not dwell upon during the day, how could it fall into his heart during his prayer?
גַּם מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב "מָנִית אַפְרוֹחַיָּא" וְכֵן "מָנִית דִּימוֹסְיָא" יֵשׁ לְהָבִין,
— Furthermore, that which was said, “I counted fledglings,” and similarly, “I counted rows of stones,” requires explanation,
שֶׁהֲלֹא אַף מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְכַוֵּין בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ עַל כָּל פָּנִים עֵינָיו סְגוּרוֹת,
— for even one who lacks internal intention in prayer at the very least keeps his eyes closed,
וְלִמְנוֹת אֶפְרוֹחִים וְשׁוּרוֹת הַבִּנְיָן צָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ הָעֵינַיִם פְּתוּחוֹת!
— and to count chicks and rows of building masonry requires that the eyes be wide open!

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 30b: “MISHNA: One may only stand and begin to pray from an approach of gravity and submission. There is a tradition that the early generations of pious men would wait one hour, in order to reach the solemn frame of mind appropriate for prayer, and then pray, so that they would focus their hearts toward their Father in Heaven. Standing in prayer is standing before God and, as such, even if the king greets him, he should not respond to him; and even if a snake is wrapped on his heel, he should not interrupt his prayer.”

Rather, it concerns one who strives to concentrate and trusts that his prayer must be answered… He thinks in his heart that his request should be fulfilled because he prayed with concentration, and comes to heartache when it is not fulfilled.” Tosafot cites the Yerushalmi’s examples of distraction but distinguishes that meaning from the presumptuous expectation condemned in this passage.

p: וְנִרְאֶה, שֶׁאַף שֶׁהָרִאשׁוֹנִים הֵבִיאוּ הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי לְעִנְיַן עִיּוּן תְּפִלָּה
— And it appears that even though the Rishonim cited the Yerushalmi in reference to flawed expectation/distraction in prayer
שֶׁאֵין מְכַוֵּון לִבּוֹ בִּתְפִלָּה,
— wherein one does not properly focus his heart in prayer,
הַיְינוּ מִפְּנֵי שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּזֶה הַלָּשׁוֹן שֶׁמּוֹרֶה בִּפְשׁוּטוֹ שֶׁלֹּא כִּיוְּונוּ בִּתְפִלָּתָם,
— that was because they framed it in this precise language which literally implies lack of focus in prayer,
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם יֵשׁ לוֹמַר כַּוָּנָה אַחֶרֶת בְּעוֹמֶק דִּבְרֵיהֶם.
— yet nevertheless one must assert an entirely different, deeper meaning in the profound depth of their words.
וְהוּא, דִּמְצִינוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ה:) בְּאַבָּא בִּנְיָמִין
— And that is, for we find (Berakhot 5b) regarding Abba Binyamin
שֶׁאָמַר שֶׁהָיָה מִצְטַעֵר עַל תְּפִלָּתִי שֶׁתְּהֵא סָמוּךְ לְמִטָּתִי,
— who said that he was anxious over his prayer that it be adjacent to his bed,
וּפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י שֶׁלֹּא לַעֲסוֹק בַּתּוֹרָה קוֹדֶם הַתְּפִלָּה,
— and Rashi explained: not to engage in Torah study prior to prayer,
וְתוֹסָפוֹת פֵּירְשׁוּ שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲשֶׂה מְלָאכָה.
— while Tosafot explained: that he should not perform physical work.
וְיֵשׁ לְהָבִין, לָמָּה נִצְטַעֵר?
— And this must be understood: why was he distressed?
הָיָה לוֹ לְהִזָּהֵר לְהִתְפַּלֵּל תֵּיכֶף בְּקוּמוֹ
— He simply should have been careful to pray immediately upon rising
וְלֹא יַעֲשֶׂה מְלָאכָה וְלֹא יִלְמוֹד קוֹדֶם!
— and neither work nor study beforehand!
אַךְ הָעִנְיָן, דַּחֲסִידִים הָרִאשׁוֹנִים הָיוּ שׁוֹהִין שָׁעָה אַחַת כְּדֵי שֶׁיְּכַוְּונוּ לִבָּם,
— However, the inner matter is that the early pious ones would linger for one hour in order to direct their hearts,
וְהַיְינוּ לְיַישֵׁר לִבָּם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה רַק לֵב אֶחָד לַאֲבִיהֶם שֶׁבַּשָּׁמָיִם,
— meaning to align their heart so that it becomes entirely unified as one heart toward their Father in Heaven,
וְלֹא יִהְיֶה בְּלִבָּם שׁוּם דָּבָר מֵעִנְיְנֵי הַגּוּף, וְזֶה מַעֲלַת הַחֲסִידִים.
— bearing no trace within of bodily concerns, and this was the elevated virtue of the pious.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מָצִינוּ מַעֲלָה גְּדוֹלָה מִזּוֹ,
— Nevertheless, we find a rung even greater than this,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם טז:):
— in the manner of what they said (there, 16b):
"וְנַשְׁכִּים וְנִמְצָא יִחוּל לְבָבֵנוּ לְיִרְאָה אֶת שְׁמֶךָ",
— “And may we arise early and find the yearning of our heart ready to revere Your Name,”
הַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִצְרָךְ שׁוּם הֲכָנָה,
— meaning that he requires no preparatory delay whatsoever,
רַק מוֹצֵא לְבָבוֹ מוּכָן לְיִרְאַת ה' כָּל הַיּוֹם וְיָכוֹל לְהִתְפַּלֵּל תֵּיכֶף.
— finding his heart spontaneously prepared for the fear of Hashem continuously and able to pray immediately.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 5b: “The Gemara returns to the topic of prayer. It was taught in a baraita that the tanna Abba Binyamin would say: All of my life I have taken great pains with regard to two things: That my prayer should be before my bed and that my bed should be placed north to south. Abba Binyamin’s statement requires explanation. With regard to his statement: That my prayer should be before my bed, the Gemara asks, what does before my bed mean? If you say that it literally means that he would stand before his bed and pray, it is difficult, as Rav Yehuda said that Rav said, and some say that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: From where is it derived that one who prays should have nothing separating between him and the wall? As it is stated: ‘And Hezekiah turned to face the wall and prayed’ (Isaiah 38:2), in order to facilitate his concentration during prayer. That being said, why would Abba Binyamin pray before his bed? Rather, do not say that before my bed refers to where he stood during prayer, but rather, say that he prayed adjacent to the time that he would retire to bed; he was careful to recite Shema and recite the evening prayer just before going to sleep (Rabbeinu Ḥananel).”

p: וְהִנֵּה הַהֲכָנָה לִתְפִלָּה בַּמִּשְׁנָה אִיתָא (שָׁם ל:):
— Now, regarding preparation for prayer, it is stated in the Mishnah (there, 30b):
"אֵין עוֹמְדִין לְהִתְפַּלֵּל אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ כּוֹבֶד רֹאשׁ",
— “One may only stand to pray from an attitude of solemn awe (koved rosh),”
וּמַיְיתֵי מִקְרָאֵי:
— and the Gemara cites verses for this:
"אֶשְׁתַּחֲוֶה אֶל הֵיכַל קָדְשְׁךָ בְּיִרְאָתֶךָ" (תְּהִלִּים ה, ח),
— “I will bow toward Your holy temple in Your fear” (Psalms 5:8),
וְכֵן "הִשְׁתַּחֲווּ לַה' בְּהַדְרַת קֹדֶשׁ" – בְּחֶרְדַּת קֹדֶשׁ,
— and likewise “Bow to Hashem in the beauty of holiness”—meaning in holy trembling,
"עִבְדוּ אֶת ה' בְּיִרְאָה" (תְּהִלִּים ב, יא).
— “Serve Hashem with fear” (Psalms 2:11).
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁעִיקַּר הַהֲכָנָה עַל יְדֵי יִרְאַת הַשֵּׁם,
— This means that the primary preparation is accomplished through fear of Hashem,
שֶׁיְּצַיֵּיר בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁבָּא לְהִתְפַּלֵּל וְלַעֲמוֹד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ.
— wherein one vividly pictures in his heart that he is coming to pray and stand directly before the King.
וּבַבָּרַיְיתָא (שָׁם לא.):
— And in the Baraita (there, 31a) it is taught:
"אֵין עוֹמְדִין לְהִתְפַּלֵּל וְכוּלֵי אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ שִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה",
— “One may only stand to pray, etc., from within the joy of a mitzvah,”
וְהַיְינוּ הָךְ דְּבָרַיְיתָא דְּ"אֵין עוֹמְדִין לְהִתְפַּלֵּל וְכוּלֵי אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ הֲלָכָה פְּסוּקָה".
— and this is identical with that other Baraita: “One may only stand to pray, etc., from within a decided halakhic ruling.”
וּמַסִּיק בַּגְּמָרָא:
— And the Gemara concludes:
רַבָּנַן עָבְדֵי כְּמַתְנִיתִין, רַב אַשִׁי עָבֵיד כְּבָרַיְיתָא.
— the Rabbis acted in accordance with the Mishnah, while Rav Ashi acted in accordance with the Baraita.
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר שֶׁזֶּה שֶׁאָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא רַבָּה:
— And it may be suggested that this is what Rabbi Chiya the Great meant by:
"מִן יוֹמָא לָא כַּוּוֹנִית",
— “In all my days I never had to direct my heart”:
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה נִצְרָךְ לְיַישֵׁר הַלֵּב וּלְכַוֵּון לִבּוֹ לַאֲבִיו שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם
— meaning that he never required intentional alignment of his heart toward his Father in Heaven
עַל יְדֵי הֲכָנָה מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אוֹ מִיִּרְאָה לִשְׁהוֹת קוֹדֶם הַתְּפִלָּה,
— via preparatory engagement in Torah words or fear by lingering before prayer,
רַק הָיָה מַשְׁכִּים וּמוֹצֵא יִחוּל לְבָבוֹ לְאַהֲבָה וּלְיִרְאָה,
— rather he would awaken and immediately find his heart yearning in natural love and reverence,
וּכִצְלוֹתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: "וְנַשְׁכִּים וְכוּלֵי".
— mirroring the prayer of Rabbi Elazar: “May we awaken, etc.”
"חַד זְמַן בָּעֵי מְכַוְּונָה",
— “On one occasion I wished to direct my heart,”
שֶׁאֵירַע שֶׁהָיָה צָרִיךְ הֲכָנָה לִתְפִלָּה לִשְׁהוֹת שָׁעָה אַחַת קוֹדֶם,
— meaning it occurred that he did require preparation for prayer by lingering for one hour beforehand,
וְנִסְתַּפֵּק אֵיזֶה הֲכָנָה יַעֲשֶׂה, אִם כְּמַתְנִיתִין אִם כְּבָרַיְיתָא.
— and he was uncertain which preparation he ought to employ: whether according to the Mishnah or according to the Baraita.
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר: "וְהִרְהַרִית בְּלִבִּי מַאן עָלֵיל קוֹמֵי מַלְכָּא קַדְמֵי, אַלְקַפְתָּא אוֹ רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא":
— And that is what he meant by: “and I reflected in my heart: who enters before the king first, the al-qafta or the Reish Galuta?”:
"אַלְקַפְתָּא" הַיְינוּ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם,
— “Al-qafta” denotes a Torah scholar,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ (זְבָחִים צו:):
— just as we find in Zevachim (96b):
"אַלְקַפְתָּא, נְקַטַן רֵיחָא אָתֵי לָהּ לְיָד",
— “Al-qafta, he who grasps fragrance has it come to his hand,”
מִשּׁוּם דַּאֲזַלַתְּ לָךְ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב שֵׁשֶׁת הֲוֵית לָךְ כְּרַב שֵׁשֶׁת,
— because you frequented the presence of Rav Sheshet you became like Rav Sheshet,
וְרַב שֵׁשֶׁת הָיָה סִינַי,
— and Rav Sheshet was designated a master of the complete Sinai tradition,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (עֵירוּבִין סז.):
— as written in Eruvin (67a):
רַב חִסְדָּא מְרַתְּעָן שִׂפְוָותֵיהּ מִמַּתְנְיָיתָא דְּרַב שֵׁשֶׁת,
— the lips of Rav Chisda would tremble from the precise traditions of Rav Sheshet,
וְזֶה עִנְיַן אַלְקַפְתָּא.
— and this is the essence of al-qafta.
וְנָקַט הַלָּשׁוֹן "נְקַטַן רֵיחָא" עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א, קנו עַמּוּד ב):
— And it employed the phrase “grasped fragrance” based on what is written (Zohar Part I, 156b):
אִינּוּן גָּרְמוּ דְּיִפּוֹק יִשָּׂשכָר לְעָלְמָא,
— they caused Issachar to emerge into the world,
בְּגִין דִּסְלִיק רֵיחָא דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא קַמֵּי קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא,
— because the fragrance of Torah ascended before the Holy One, blessed be He,
הֲדָא הוּא דִכְתִיב: "הַדּוּדָאִים נָתְנוּ רֵיחַ" (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ז, יד),
— that is what is written: “The mandrakes gave forth fragrance” (Song of Songs 7:14),
וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת פח:):
— and along the lines of what they taught (Shabbat 88b):
שֶׁמִּכָּל דִּבּוּר וְכוּלֵי נִתְמַלֵּא כָּל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ בְּשָׂמִים.
— that with every divine utterance the entire world was filled with fragrance.
וְרֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא הוּא שֵׁבֶט מוֹשֵׁל,
— And the Reish Galuta represents the governing staff of royal power,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (סַנְהֶדְרִין ה.):
— as written in Sanhedrin (5a):
"לֹא יָסוּר שֵׁבֶט מִיהוּדָה" – אֵלּוּ רָאשֵׁי גָלִיּוֹת שֶׁבְּבָבֶל שֶׁרוֹדִין אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּשֵׁבֶט;
— “The scepter shall not depart from Judah”—these are the Exilarchs in Babylon who govern Israel with the staff;
וְכֵן מָצִינוּ (חֻלִּין צב.):
— and similarly we find in Chullin (92a):
"כִּי שָׂרִיתָ עִם אֱלֹהִים וְעִם אֲנָשִׁים" (בְּרֵאשִׁית לב, כט) –
— “For you have striven with godlike beings and with men” (Genesis 32:29) –
רָמַז לוֹ וְכוּלֵי רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא שֶׁבְּבָבֶל וְנָשִׂיא שֶׁבְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל.
— He hinted to him, etc., the Exilarch in Babylon and the Prince (Nasi) in the Land of Israel.
וְהַיְינוּ דְּנָשִׂיא הוּא בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
— And this means the Nasi represents authority in Torah,
וּכְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י שֶׁסְּמוּכִים הֵם נִקְרְאוּ "אֱלֹהִים",
— and according to Rashi's commentary, ordained judges are titled “elohim”,
וְרֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא הַיְינוּ "אֲנָשִׁים" שֶׁהוּא שֵׁבֶט מֶמְשָׁלָה.
— while the Exilarch corresponds to “men”, representing the staff of political rulership.
וּמָצִינוּ בַּגְּמָרָא (בְּרָכוֹת לד:):
— And we find in the Gemara (Berakhot 34b):
הַמֶּלֶךְ, כֵּיוָן שֶׁכָּרַע שׁוּב אֵינוֹ זוֹקֵף,
— the king, once he bows, does not erect himself again,
שֶׁהוּא מָלֵא יִרְאָה וְהַכְנָעָה וָפַחַד.
— for he stands filled with awe, submission, and dread.
וְזֶה שֶׁנִּסְתַּפֵּק רַבִּי חִיָּיא:
— And this was the contemplative doubt of Rabbi Chiya:
אֵיזוֹ הֲכָנָה יַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁיְּכַוֵּין וְיְיַשֵּׁר לִבּוֹ לַאֲבִיו שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם,
— which spiritual preparation should he enact to focus and align his heart toward his Father in Heaven:
אִם עַל יְדֵי כּוֹבֶד הָרֹאשׁ וְהַכְנָעָה וָפַחַד,
— whether through solemn awe, submission, and fear,
שֶׁעַל זֶה מְרַמֵּז מַדְרֵגַת רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא וּכְמַתְנִיתִין,
— which the rung of the Exilarch alludes to, matching the Mishnah;
אוֹ שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה הַהֲכָנָה לְכַוֵּון לִבּוֹ מִתּוֹךְ דְּבַר הֲלָכָה פְּסוּקָה כְּבָרַיְיתָא,
— or whether he should make the preparation to focus his heart from within a clear halakhic ruling according to the Baraita,
שֶׁעַל זֶה מְרַמֵּז אַלְקַפְתָּא כָּאָמוּר.
— which al-qafta alludes to, as stated.
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר: "וְאָמְרִי: מַאן עָלֵיל קָמֵי מַלְכָּא קַדְמֵי, אַלְקַפְתָּא",
— And that is what he meant by: “And I said: who enters before the King first, al-qafta,”
שֶׁזֶּה מְרַמֵּז מִתּוֹךְ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
— which alludes to entering from within words of Torah,
"אוֹ רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא", שֶׁמְּרַמֵּז עַל יִרְאָה.
— “or the Reish Galuta,” which alludes to fear.
וּבֶאֱמֶת שְׁנֵיהֶם אֶחָד,
— And in truth both are one,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ג, יז):
— as is written (Avot 3:17):
"אִם אֵין חָכְמָה אֵין יִרְאָה, אִם אֵין יִרְאָה אֵין חָכְמָה",
— “If there is no wisdom there is no fear; if there is no fear there is no wisdom,”
רַק שֶׁנִּסְתַּפֵּק רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּמֶּה יִהְיֶה הַתְחָלַת הָאִתְעָרוּתָא,
— only that Rabbi Chiya weighed which element should be the initiator of the spiritual awakening:
אִם מִתּוֹרָה אוֹ מִיִּרְאָה וְהַכְנָעָה,
— whether from Torah or from awe and submission,
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר: "מַאן עָלֵיל קָמֵי מַלְכָּא קַדְמֵי וְכוּלֵי", וְהַיְינוּ מַה לְּהַקְדִּים.
— and this is what he phrased: “Who enters before the King first, etc.,” meaning what to prioritize.

p: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר אַבָּא בִּנְיָמִין שֶׁהָיָה מִצְטַעֵר עַל תְּפִלָּתוֹ שֶׁתְּהֵא סָמוּךְ לְמִטָּתוֹ,
— And this is what Abba Binyamin meant in being distressed that his prayer be adjacent to his bed,
וְזֶה שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י שֶׁלֹּא לַעֲשׂוֹת מְלָאכָה אוֹ לַעֲסוֹק בַּתּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי.
— which explains Rashi's interpretation: not to perform labor or engage in Torah, etc.
וְהַיְינוּ כְּעֵין צְלוֹתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר:
— And that is similar to the prayer of Rabbi Elazar:
"וְנַשְׁכִּים וְנִמְצָא יִחוּל לְבָבֵנוּ לְיִרְאָה",
— “May we arise early and find the yearning of our heart ready to revere,”
וְהוּא שֶׁלֹּא יִצְטָרֵךְ שׁוּם הֲכָנָה לְכַוֵּון וּלְיַישֵׁר לִבּוֹ לַאֲבִיו שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם,
— which is that he should require no intermediary preparation to direct and align his heart to his Father in Heaven,
לֹא עַל יְדֵי תוֹרָה וְלֹא עַל יְדֵי עֲבוֹדָה וְצִיּוּר הַיִּרְאָה וְהַהַכְנָעָה בַּלֵּב בִּשְׁהִיּוּת שָׁעָה אַחַת,
— neither through Torah nor through devotional service and mentally fashioning fear and submission in the heart by lingering an hour,
רַק יִמְצָא לְבָבוֹ מְכוּוָּן וּמְיוּשָּׁר לֵב אֶחָד לַאֲבִיו שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם
— rather that he find his heart spontaneously directed and upright as one heart toward his Father in Heaven
וְיוּכַל לְהִתְפַּלֵּל תֵּיכֶף בְּקוּמוֹ סָמוּךְ לְמִטָּתוֹ,
— and be able to pray instantly upon rising, right next to his bed,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא רַבָּה: "מִן יוֹמָא לָא כַּוּוֹנִית", וְכַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
— and as Rabbi Chiya the Great said: “In all my days I never had to direct my heart,” as mentioned above.

p: שְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: "אֲנָא מָנִית אַפְרוֹחַיָּא",
— Shmuel said: “I counted fledglings,”
הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (תִּקּוּנֵי זֹהַר תִּקּוּנָא י):
— which aligns with what is written (Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 10):
"וְאוֹרַיְיתָא בְּלָא דְּחִילוּ וּרְחִימוּ לָא פָּרְחַת לְעֵילָא וְכוּלֵי,
— “And Torah without awe and love does not fly upward, etc.,
וּמִצְוָה בְּלָא דְּחִילוּ וּרְחִימוּ לָא יָכִילַת לְסַלְּקָא וְכוּלֵי",
— and a mitzvah without awe and love cannot ascend, etc.,”
וְהַיְינוּ "מָנִית אַפְרוֹחַיָּא",
— and this is the meaning of “I counted fledglings”:
שֶׁהָיָה מוֹנֶה בְּדִבְרֵי תְּפִלָּתוֹ הַיִּרְאָה וְהָאַהֲבָה שֶׁבּוֹ
— that he was measuring within the words of his prayer the fear and love embedded in it
שֶׁעַל יְדֵיהֶם תְּהֵא פָּרְחָא לְעֵילָא,
— through which it flies upward,
וְזֶהוּ מְרוּמָּז בְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב "אַפְרוֹחַיָּא".
— and this is alluded to by his expression “fledglings” (winged birds).
רַבִּי בּוּן בַּר חִיָּיא אָמַר: "מָנִית דִּימוֹסְיָא",
— Rabbi Bun bar Chiya said: “I counted rows of masonry,”
הוּא עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (סֵפֶר יְצִירָה סוֹף פֶּרֶק ד)
— which is based upon what is written (Sefer Yetzirah, end of chapter 4)
שֶׁקָּרָא הָאוֹתִיּוֹת "אֲבָנִים",
— which designates the Hebrew letters as “stones”,
וְצֵירוּף אוֹתִיּוֹת הֵם כְּמוֹ שׁוּרַת הַבִּנְיָן
— and the combinations of letters resemble rows of a building
שֶׁנַּעֲשֶׂה מִכַּמָּה אֲבָנִים תֵּיבָה שְׁלֵימָה,
— wherein from several stones an entire word is constructed;
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר: "מָנִית דִּימוֹסְיָא", שֶׁהָיָה מוֹנֶה תֵּיבוֹת הַתְּפִלָּה.
— and this is what he meant by “I counted rows of masonry,” that he was counting the words of the prayer.

p: וְהַהֶבְדֵּל בֵּינֵיהֶם הוּא,
— And the distinction between them is
דְּאִיכָּא "תְּפִלָּה לֶעָנִי" וְאִיכָּא "תְּפִלָּה לְמֹשֶׁה אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים"
— that there is a “prayer of the afflicted” and there is a “prayer of Moses the man of God”
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק א, קסח עַמּוּד ב),
— (as written in Zohar Part I, 168b),
וְהַחִילּוּק בֵּינֵיהֶם הוּא כְּעֵין מַחֲלוֹקֶת (סוֹטָה ה.):
— and the difference between them mirrors the dispute in Sotah (5a):
רַב חִסְדָּא וְרַב הוּנָא,
— between Rav Chisda and Rav Huna,
חַד אָמַר: "אִתִּי דַּכָּא",
— one said: “The contrite ascends with Me,”
וְחַד אָמַר: "אֲנִי אֶת דַּכָּא".
— and the other said: “I dwell with the contrite.”
תְּפִלָּה לֶעָנִי הוּא "אֲנִי אֶת דַּכָּא",
— The prayer of the afflicted embodies “I dwell with the contrite,”
שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַרְכִּין שְׁכִינָתוֹ
— where Hashem lowers His Shechinah
וְשׁוֹכֵן בְּתוֹךְ לֵב הַמִּתְפַּלֵּל וּבְתוֹךְ אוֹתִיּוֹת הַתְּפִלָּה.
— and dwells within the heart of the worshiper and within the letters of the prayer.
וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת לד:):
— And along the lines of what they stated (Berakhot 34b):
"אִם שְׁגוּרָה תְּפִלָּתִי בְּפִי יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי שֶׁהוּא מְקוּבָּל",
— “If my prayer flows fluently in my mouth, I know that it is accepted,”
וּבַגְּמָרָא יָלֵיף מִדִּכְתִיב: "בּוֹרֵא נִיב שְׂפָתָיִם וְגוֹמֵר" (יְשַׁעְיָה נז, יט);
— and the Gemara derives this from the verse: “Creator of the fruit of the lips, etc.” (Isaiah 57:19);
וּבַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי שָׁם הַגִּירְסָא:
— and in the Yerushalmi there the text reads:
"אִם עָשׂוּ שִׂפְתוֹתָיו שֶׁל אָדָם תְּנוּבָה יְהֵא מְבוּשָּׂר שֶׁנִּשְׁמַע תְּפִלָּתוֹ",
— “If a person’s lips produced fruit, let him be assured that his prayer is heard,”
וְדָרַשׁ גַּם כֵּן מִדִּכְתִיב "בּוֹרֵא נִיב שְׂפָתָיִם וְגוֹמֵר";
— and it expounds this likewise from the verse “Creator of the fruit of the lips, etc.”;
וְכֵן בִּמְדְרַשׁ רַבָּה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה טז, ט):
— and so too in Midrash Rabbah (Vayikra Rabbah 16:9):
"אִם הֵנִיבוּ שְׂפָתָיו בִּתְפִלָּה וְכוּלֵי, מַה טַּעַם? בּוֹרֵא נִיב שְׂפָתָיִם וְגוֹמֵר".
— “If his lips bore fruit in prayer, etc., what is the reason? ‘Creator of the fruit of the lips, etc.’”
וְהוּא, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הַבּוֹרֵא נִיב שְׂפָתַיִם
— And this signifies that Hashem, blessed be He, is the One Who creates the fruit of the lips
שֶׁיָּנוּבוּ שְׂפָתוֹתָיו וְיִהְיֶה תְּפִלָּתוֹ שְׁגוּרָה בְּפִיו.
— so that his lips bear fruit and his prayer flows fluently in his mouth.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר רַבֵּינוּ רַבִּי אֱלִימֶלֶךְ זְכוּתוֹ יָגֵן עָלֵינוּ אָמֵן
— And as our master Rabbi Elimelech, may his merit protect us, Amen, taught
עַל מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב "אִם שְׁגוּרָה" – שֶׁהוּא מִלְּשׁוֹן שְׁלִיחוּת,
— on that which was stated “if it is fluently dispatched (shgura)”—that it stems from the concept of a mission (sheliḥut),
שֶׁשָּׁלַח הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַתְּפִלָּה בְּפִיו;
— for Hashem Himself dispatched the prayer into his mouth;
וְזֶה מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּגְּמָרָא (שָׁם ז.):
— and this is what is stated in the Gemara (there, 7a):
"בְּבֵית תְּפִלָּתִי" (יְשַׁעְיָה נו, ז) – מִכָּאן שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִתְפַּלֵּל,
— “In My house of prayer” (Isaiah 56:7)—from here we derive that the Holy One, blessed be He, prays,
וְהַיְינוּ בְּתוֹךְ פִּיפִיּוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁשּׁוֹלֵחַ הַתְּפִלָּה בְּפִיהֶם, עַד כָּאן דִּבְרֵי קָדְשׁוֹ.
— meaning inside the mouths of Israel, Hashem sending the prayer into their mouths, thus far his holy words.
וְזֶה שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ מִמַּה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "בּוֹרֵא נִיב שְׂפָתָיִם",
— And this is what they expounded from “Creator of the fruit of the lips”,
וְאַף לְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י שֶׁהַנִּיב בָּרִיא בְּאָדָם וְכוּלֵי,
— and even according to Rashi's interpretation that speech is soundly formed within man, etc.,
הַמְכֻוָּון גַּם כֵּן שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹלֵחַ זֶה,
— the intended meaning is likewise that Hashem sends this,
שֶׁמַּה שֶּׁהַתְּפִלָּה שְׁגוּרָה בְּפִיו הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
— in that the prayer’s fluency in his mouth originates from Hashem, blessed be He,
וּכִדִכְתִיב: "בּוֹרֵא נִיב וְגוֹמֵר", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי וּמִדְרָשׁ.
— as it is written: “Creator of the fruit, etc.,” and as brought in the Yerushalmi and Midrash.
וְעוֹד אָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי וּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה שָׁם:
— Furthermore they said in the Yerushalmi and Midrash Rabbah there:
"אִם כִּיוַּוֹנְתָּ אֶת לִבְּךָ בִּתְפִלָּה תְּהֵא מְבוּשָּׂר שֶׁנִּשְׁמְעָה תְּפִלָּתְךָ,
— “If you directed your heart in prayer, be assured that your prayer is heard,
וּמַה טַּעַם? 'תָּכִין לִבָּם תַּקְשִׁיב אָזְנֶךָ' (תְּהִלִּים י, יז)".
— and what is the reason? ‘You prepare their heart; You incline Your ear’ (Psalms 10, 17).”
וְהַיְינוּ גַּם כֵּן שֶׁאַף כַּוָּנַת וְיַשְׁרוּת הַלֵּב שֶׁלֹּא יְהֵא מְפוּזָּר בְּעִנְיְנֵי הַגּוּף,
— And this also means that even the focused alignment of the heart not to be scattered across bodily pursuits,
זֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן עִיקַּר הַסַּיַּיעְתָּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
— this too is primarily divine assistance from Hashem, blessed be He,
אַחַר הֲכָנַת הָאָדָם מִצִּדּוֹ בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא,
— following man’s initial preparatory awakening from below,
וְכִדִכְתִיב: "תָּכִין לִבָּם" – תָּכִין דַּיְיקָא.
— and as it is written: “You prepare their heart”—You prepare, specifically.
וְזֶהוּ "אֲנִי אֶת דַּכָּא",
— And this represents “I dwell with the contrite,”
שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹכֵן בְּתוֹךְ תֵּיבוֹת הַתְּפִלָּה,
— wherein Hashem rests within the very words of prayer,
וְזֶהוּ תְּפִלָּה לֶעָנִי,
— and this is the prayer of the afflicted,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ
— and as written in the holy Zohar
דְּעָנִי אִתְדְּבַק בְּמִסְכְּנוּתֵיהּ כְּמַאן דְּלֵית לֵיהּ מִגַּרְמֵיהּ כְּלוּם,
— that the poor man clings in his destitution like one who has nothing of his own,
וּכְעִנְיַן מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אֲדֹנָי שְׂפָתַי תִּפְתָּח וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים נא, יז).
— and in the sense of the verse: “O Lord, open my lips, etc.” (Psalms 51:17).
וּתְפִלָּה לְמֹשֶׁה אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים הוּא כְּשֶׁזּוֹכֶה "אִתִּי דַּכָּא",
— And the prayer of Moses the man of God is when one merits “the contrite ascends with Me,”
שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַגְבִּיהוֹ עַד שֶׁשּׁוֹכֵן לְמַעְלָה אֶצְלוֹ.
— where Hashem elevates him until he dwells Above in His presence.
וְזֶה מַה שֶּׁאָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: "אֲנָא מָנִית אַפְרוֹחַיָּא",
— And this is what Shmuel meant: “I counted fledglings,”
דְּדִבְרֵי הַתְּפִלָּה פָּרְחִין לְעֵילָא עַל יְדֵי הַדְּחִילוּ וּרְחִימוּ.
— for the words of prayer take flight upward via awe and love.
וְרַבִּי בּוּן אָמַר שֶׁהוּא לֹא זָכָה לָזֶה,
— While Rabbi Bun said that he did not merit that lofty elevation,
רַק שֶׁתְּפִלָּתוֹ תְּפִלָּה לֶעָנִי,
— but that his prayer remained the prayer of the afflicted,
שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: הַכִּיוּוּן וְיַשְׁרוּת הַלֵּב וְנִיב שְׂפָתַיִם,
— wherein everything is directly from Hashem: the directed alignment of the heart and the fruit of the lips,
וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹכֵן בְּתוֹךְ תֵּיבוֹת הַתְּפִלָּה.
— and Hashem dwells inside the words of the prayer.
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר: "אֲנָא מָנִית דִּימוֹסְיָא",
— And this is why he said: “I counted rows of stones,”
דְּהַיְינוּ תֵּיבוֹת הַתְּפִלָּה שֶׁהֵם כְּשׁוּרוֹת בִּנְיָן כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹכֵן בָּהֶם,
— meaning the words of prayer which are like rows of masonry as noted above in which Hashem abides,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְפַּלֵּל בְּתוֹךְ פִּיּוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל.
— and as it was stated that Hashem prays within the mouths of Israel.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 5a: “The Gemara continues the discussion of arrogance, and its converse, humility. The verse states: ‘For thus says the High and Lofty One that inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: I dwell in the high and holy place, also with him that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones’ (Isaiah 57:15). Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda offered differing interpretations of this verse. One says that the verse means: Together with Me is the person who is contrite and humble. In other words, God elevates the humble. And one says that the verse means: I, God, descend, and am found together with the person who is contrite and humble.”

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 34b: “MISHNA: Concluding its discussion of the halakhot of prayer, the mishna discusses less practical aspects of prayer. One who prays and realizes that he erred in his prayer, it is a bad omen for him; it indicates to him that his prayer was not accepted. And if he who erred is the communal prayer leader, it is a bad omen for those who sent him, because a person’s agent has legal status equivalent to his own. On a similar note, they said about Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa that he would pray on behalf of the sick and immediately after his prayer he would say: This one shall recover from his illness and live and this one shall die. When they said to him: From where do you know? He said to them: If my prayer is fluent in my mouth as I recite it and there are no errors, I know that my prayer is accepted. And if not, I know that my prayer is rejected.”

p: וְזֶה מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב: "כִּינּוּסוֹ וְכִינּוּס בָּנָיו"
— And this explains the passage: “his gathering and the gathering of his sons”:
דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁאִיקוֹנִין שֶׁלּוֹ קָבוּעַ בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד
— for Jacob our father, peace be upon him, whose visage is engraved on the Throne of Glory
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (מִדְרַשׁ רַבָּה בְּמִדְבַּר רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה ד) שֶׁהוּא דְּמוּת אָדָם שֶׁעַל הַכִּסֵּא,
— as written (Midrash Rabbah Bemidbar 4:1) that he is the likeness of the man upon the Throne,
וְכִינּוּסוֹ לִתְפִלָּה, שֶׁהוּא כִּיוּוּן וְיַשְׁרוּת לִבּוֹ לִתְפִלָּה,
— and his gathering to prayer, which is the focused alignment of his heart for prayer,
הוּא כִּתְפִלָּה לְמֹשֶׁה שֶׁעוֹלָה לְמַעְלָה "דַּכָּא אִתִּי".
— is like the prayer of Moses that ascends Above, “the contrite ascends with Me.”
וְכִינּוּס בָּנָיו, שֶׁלֹּא זָכוּ לְמִדַּת אֱמֶת כָּמוֹהוּ,
— While the gathering of his sons, who did not merit the quintessential attribute of Truth like him,
רַק עַל יְדֵי אֱמוּנָה מַשִּׂיגִים הַיִּחוּד יִחוּדָא תַּתָּאָה,
— only attaining through faith the lower divine unity (yiḥuda tata'ah),
וְכִינּוּס בָּנָיו לִתְפִלָּה הוּא מֵעֵין תְּפִלָּה לֶעָנִי
— so the gathering of his sons to prayer is in the mode of the prayer of the afflicted
דְּלֵית לֵיהּ מִגַּרְמֵיהּ כְּלוּם, "אֲנִי אֶת דַּכָּא".
— who has nothing of his own, “I dwell with the contrite.”
וְעַל כֵּן חִילֵּק אוֹתָם בִּמְדְרַשׁ רַבָּה,
— Therefore Midrash Rabbah differentiated them,
שֶׁאֵינוֹ דּוֹמֶה כִּינּוּסוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לְכִינּוּס בָּנָיו,
— showing that the gathering of our father Jacob, peace be upon him, is not identical to the gathering of his sons,
וּשְׁנֵיהֶם הִצִּילוּ מִיַּד עֵשָׂו.
— and yet both delivered them from the hand of Esau.
וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "בְּזַעֲקֵךְ יַצִּילוּךְ קִבּוּצַיִךְ",
— And this is what Scripture states: “When you cry out, let your assemblies save you,”
דְּכִינּוּסוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אֵין צָרִיךְ זְעָקָה וּצְעָקָה,
— for the gathering of Jacob our father, peace be upon him, requires neither screaming nor outward crying out,
רַק עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא: "מִן יוֹמָא לָא כַּוּוֹנִית",
— rather in the manner of what Rabbi Chiya said: “In all my days I never had to direct my heart,”
שֶׁהוּא שֶׁמָּצָא יִחוּל לְבָבוֹ מוּכָן לְיִרְאָה וְכַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל,
— finding the yearning of his heart spontaneously ready for reverence as noted above,
וְהוּא אָמַר: "מַשִּׁיב הָרוּחַ" וְנָשֵׁיב זִיקָא וְכוּלֵי בַּאֲמִירָה בְּעָלְמָא.
— and he merely said “He causes the wind to blow” and the wind blew, etc., with a mere quiet utterance.
וְאַף שֶׁמָּצִינוּ: "וְהָיָה טֶרֶם יִקְרָאוּ וַאֲנִי אֶעֱנֶה" (יְשַׁעְיָה סה, כד),
— And even though we find: “And it shall come to pass that before they call, I will answer” (Isaiah 65:24),
רַק גַּם זֶה אֵינוֹ שְׁבָחוֹ שֶׁל צִיבּוּר,
— nevertheless even this is not the supreme praise of the community,
וּשְׁבָחוֹ שֶׁל צִיבּוּר הוּא: אָמַר "מַשִּׁיב הָרוּחַ" וְנָשֵׁיב זִיקָא, אָמַר "מוֹרִיד הַגֶּשֶׁם" וַאֲתָא מִטְרָא
— for the supreme praise of the community is: he said “He causes the wind to blow” and the wind blew, he said “He causes the rain to fall” and the rain arrived
(וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב תַּעֲנִית כה:),
— (and as written in Ta'anit 25b),
וְכִתְפִלַּת רַבִּי חִיָּיא וּבָנָיו.
— and like the prayer of Rabbi Chiya and his sons.
וְכִינּוּס בָּנָיו עַל דֶּרֶךְ תְּפִלָּה לֶעָנִי,
— Whereas the gathering of his sons operates in the mode of the prayer of the afflicted,
וְזֶהוּ צָרִיךְ זְעָקָה,
— and this does require crying out,
וְזֶהוּ "בְּזַעֲקֵךְ יַצִּילוּךְ קִבּוּצַיִךְ",
— and this is “When you cry out, let your assemblies save you,”
שֶׁהוּא כִּינּוּס בָּנָיו לִתְפִלָּה, וְכָאָמוּר.
— referring to the gathering of his sons for prayer, as stated.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Sod Yesharim, Sukkot §34, paragraph 2: “No individual soul on its own can possess completely perfected refinement, for who can say, “I have purified my heart”? Only when a person includes himself in the community can he be fully refined, because the collective possesses complete refinement: what one lacks, another reveals. Every soul of Israel contains a precious point absent from another soul, in which it is more refined and distinguished than all Israel. That precious point does not come to teach about itself alone, but about the whole community. When the individuals unite as a community, each therefore teaches the other, until no deficiency remains in the community. For this reason the Sages greatly praise communal prayer. Prayer is a person’s request that God fulfill his heart’s desires, and it requires clarification in three respects: first, that his request not oppose God’s will; second, that it not oppose the community; third, that it not oppose his own human form, as explained elsewhere. … For this reason the holy Arizal wrote that before prayer one must accept the commandment “Love your neighbor as yourself,” because through this his prayer will be included within the community. Concerning this the holy Zohar, Vayechi 234, says: “He turned to the prayer of the destitute”—this is an individual included among the many; “say that this is Jacob.” This is the attribute of our father Jacob: always to unite with the community of Israel. Whoever possesses this quality of including himself within the community always has communal prayer.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Rav Tzadok distinguishes Jacob’s fully unified heart from his sons’ gathered prayer. Sod Yesharim explains why the latter gathering has its own spiritual force: different souls contribute distinctive virtues that complete one another and purify what is being requested.
